blocks.text: Every linked list operation is built from the same three moves: **walk** with a pointer, **save** the arrow you're about to change, and **re-point** an arrow. This lesson builds the everyday operations from those moves, in four languages.
1. Build a list from an array

Most problems hand you a list, but for testing you'll often want to build one. The trick is a **dummy** node in front: it gives the loop a place to attach the first real node, so there's no special case for an empty list.

blocks.code:
def from_array(values):
    dummy = ListNode(0)        # placeholder in front of the head
    tail = dummy
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)    # attach a new node at the end
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next          # the real head

blocks.text: There's no `length` field: to know the size you walk to the end and count. That's **O(n)** — remember it, because several problems need the length first.

blocks.code:
def length(head):
    count = 0
    curr = head
    while curr is not None:
        count += 1
        curr = curr.next
    return count

blocks.text: To insert at position `pos`, walk to the node **just before** it (`prev`), then make two arrow changes — in this order:

blocks.alt: Inserting 25 between 20 and 30. Step 1: the new node's next points to 30. Step 2: 20's next points to the new node. Doing step 2 first would lose the link to 30.

elements.text: do 1 before 2 — otherwise the link to 30 is gone
elements.originalText: do 1 before 2 — otherwise the link to 30 is gone

blocks.caption: Try positions 0 (the front), the middle, and the length of the list (the end).

blocks.code:
def insert_at(head, pos, x):
    node = ListNode(x)
    if pos == 0:               # new head
        node.next = head
        return node
    prev = head
    for _ in range(pos - 1):   # node before the spot
        prev = prev.next
    node.next = prev.next      # 1. hold on to the rest
    prev.next = node           # 2. hook the new node in
    return head

blocks.text: You can't delete a node by pointing at it — you have to change the arrow **coming into** it. So walk with `prev` until `prev.next` is the node to remove, then make `prev.next` skip over it.

blocks.alt: Deleting 30 from 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40: the arrow from 20 now curves over 30 straight to 40, and 30 is left with nothing pointing to it.

elements.text: nothing points to 30 any more, so it is gone
elements.originalText: nothing points to 30 any more, so it is gone

blocks.caption: Try deleting the head, a middle node, and a value that isn't there.

blocks.text: In C++ there's no garbage collector: also `delete` the removed node to free its memory. The other three languages free it for you once nothing points to it.

Notice how insert and delete both needed a special case for the **head**, because the head has no `prev`. A **dummy** node placed in front of the head removes that special case: now every real node, including the head, has a node before it. Many interview solutions start with `dummy = new ListNode(0); dummy.next = head` and end with `return dummy.next`.

blocks.alt: A dummy node in front of the list 10 -> 20 -> 30. With the dummy, even the head node 10 has a previous node, so insert and delete need no special case. The function returns dummy.next.

items: **Losing the rest of the list.** Changing `curr.next` before saving it cuts the list in two. Save `next` first, change the arrow second.
**Forgetting null checks.** `curr.next.val` crashes when `curr.next` is null. Every loop condition should guard the pointer it's about to follow.
**Not returning the new head.** If an operation can change the head (inserting at 0, deleting the first node), the caller must use the returned head.
**Moving the head while walking.** Walk with a separate `curr` pointer; if you move `head` itself, you lose the start of the list.

blocks.alt: Operation costs for a singly linked list: insert or delete at the head O(1); insert or delete after a node you hold O(1); reach index i O(i); search for a value O(n); insert at the tail O(n), or O(1) if you keep a tail pointer; length O(n).
